name: wuppiefuzz
desc: Coverage-guided REST API fuzzer developed on top of LibAFL
why: Coverage-guided fuzzing of REST APIs built on LibAFL, a genuinely clever way to watch a service crack under feedback.

brief.what_it_is: WuppieFuzz is a coverage-guided fuzzer for REST APIs, built on LibAFL and developed by TNO. You give it an OpenAPI specification (YAML) and a running target service, and it generates and mutates HTTP requests against that API, using coverage feedback to steer the search. Output goes to a timestamped subdirectory under reports/ when you pass --report: endpoint coverage (from the spec alone) and, for JaCoCo targets, code coverage. A database of request data is also written, which can be explored in a Grafana dashboard.
brief.why_it_exists: TNO says it targets a wide audience of end-users, with a strong focus on ease-of-use, explainability of the discovered flaws and modularity. The README says it supports black box, grey box and white box testing.
brief.how_it_works: The OpenAPI spec tells WuppieFuzz how to build and mutate requests, and the target must already be running (instrumented, if you want code coverage). Coverage from the target, such as a JaCoCo agent or LCOV for Python, feeds back into the fuzzing loop. Endpoint coverage needs only the spec; code coverage needs a mapping from coverage data to source files.

commands_seen.context: Builds the WuppieFuzz Docker image locally, tagged wuppiefuzz:local.

commands_seen.cmd:
docker run \
  --network host \
  -v ./fuzzing-folder:/fuzzing-folder \  # The folder will be populated with wuppiefuzz outputs
  -w /fuzzing-folder \
  wuppiefuzz:local fuzz --timeout 60 --report openapi.json
commands_seen.context: Runs the container with host networking (needed when fuzzing a service running locally, outside Docker), mounts a folder with the OpenAPI spec, and fuzzes for 60 seconds with a report. The README's own comment on the -v line is included as written.
Shows the help text with required parameters and flags, including the usage line Usage: wuppiefuzz [OPTIONS] [OPENAPI_SPEC.YAML].
Example run against a Java target with the JaCoCo agent attached, giving the spec, the JaCoCo coverage format and the classes directory.
Combines a YAML config file with command-line flags; the command-line --timeout=10 overrides the value set in the config file.

commands_seen.context: Installs general build tools needed to build the project from source on Debian/Ubuntu.
Installs the Rust toolchain via rustup, a development prerequisite.
System libraries for a development build that avoids vendored dependencies (Debian/Ubuntu).
Installs Z3 4.15+ via Homebrew; the README says apt's libz3-dev is too old for the z3 crate.

brief.install_notes: Install with brew install wuppiefuzz or grab a binary from the GitHub releases page. To build from source you need build-essential, pkg-config and cmake, plus Rust via rustup. By default, C dependencies (OpenSSL, SQLite, Z3) are vendored, so a plain cargo build works. For faster dev builds you can link system libraries instead, which needs libssl-dev and libsqlite3-dev, plus Z3 4.15+ (the README recommends Homebrew on Linux, and the Homebrew library path must be added to LIBRARY_PATH and LD_LIBRARY_PATH). Fedora 42+ uses openssl-devel, sqlite-devel and z3-devel; macOS uses brew install openssl sqlite z3. Docker is an option too: build the image locally and mount a folder containing the OpenAPI spec. Configuration can come from a YAML file via --config; example configs for JaCoCo (Java) and LCOV (Python) are in example_configs/. The target must be started before WuppieFuzz runs.
brief.standout: It covers black box, grey box and white box REST API fuzzing in one tool. Endpoint coverage comes from the OpenAPI spec alone, so you get a coverage figure even without instrumenting the target. A Grafana dashboard visualises the request database from a campaign.
brief.caveats: Code coverage is currently supported only for JaCoCo; the README says more formats are planned. The target must be instrumented and running beforehand. Z3 4.15+ is needed for system-library builds, and most Linux distribution packages are too old, so Homebrew is recommended. Docker needs host networking to reach a service running on the host. The README does not state a license beyond Apache-2.0, a last release date, or a last commit date. The brew formula has no caveats.
quotes: targeting a wide audience of end-users, with a strong focus on ease-of-use, explainability of the discovered flaws and modularity
WuppieFuzz supports all three settings of testing (black box, grey box and white box).
By default, WuppieFuzz vendors its C dependencies (OpenSSL, SQLite, Z3) so that a regular `cargo build` works out of the box.

entry.title: WuppieFuzz
entry.tldr: A coverage-guided fuzzer that reads an OpenAPI spec and mutates HTTP requests against a running service, using feedback to find where the API breaks.
entry.deeper_look:
WuppieFuzz takes an OpenAPI specification in YAML and a target service that is already running. It builds HTTP requests from the spec, mutates them, and fires them at the API. It is built on LibAFL, the Rust fuzzing library, and developed by TNO.

The idea underneath is feedback-driven fuzzing, which is usually applied to binaries, moved up to the HTTP layer. If the target is instrumented, coverage data (a JaCoCo agent for Java, LCOV for Python) flows back into the loop and steers which requests get mutated next. Without instrumentation you still get endpoint coverage, which is computed from the spec alone, so you can see which parts of the API your campaign has touched.

It supports black box, grey box and white box testing. TNO says it targets "a wide audience of end-users, with a strong focus on ease-of-use, explainability of the discovered flaws and modularity". With `--report`, results land in a timestamped folder under reports/. A database of request data is also written, which you can explore in a Grafana dashboard.
entry.install:
brew install wuppiefuzz
# Needs a running target service and its OpenAPI spec. Code coverage needs an instrumented target (JaCoCo only for now). Binaries are also on the GitHub releases page, and a Docker image can be built from the repo.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the usage line and the required parameters and flags.
Fuzzes the running service described by the spec for 60 seconds and writes an endpoint coverage report under reports/.
Combines a YAML config file with command-line flags; the command-line timeout overrides the config value.

entry.whats_unique: It covers black box, grey box and white box REST fuzzing in one tool. You get an endpoint coverage figure from the spec alone, with no instrumentation of the target.
entry.caveats: Code coverage works only with JaCoCo for now, the target must be started and instrumented beforehand, and the brief does not show a last release or commit date.
